messages.subject: Fwd: Re: BioGeoBEARS error in expokit_dgpadm_Qmat() when running default DEC model
parts:
I should add to this answer:

Just as you can access the variable type for "j", the
initial starting value of "j", etc., like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","type"]
= "free"

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","init"]
= 0.01


...you can access the "min" and "max" for "j" (or "d", "e",
whatever), like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","min"]

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","max"]

Often, narrowing the limits a teeny bit fixes NaN/Inf
problems during the ML search.

You can access the full parameters table with:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table


Cheers,
Nick


On Friday, February 14, 2014, X wrote:

Dear Nick,

I hope you can help me out with an error I get when
running BioGeoBEARS.

I run BioGeoBEARS (with all the latest fixes) on a Mac
10.8.5 using the most recent version of R and R studio.
When I try running the default DEC model with my own
data (8 areas, 96 taxa, max_range_size=4)
check_BioGeoBEARS_run returns no errors, but when I
continue to run the DEC model it runs at first, but
later I get the following error:

Error in rexpokit::expokit_dgpadm_Qmat(Qmat = Qmat, t =
times, transpose_needed) : NA/NaN/Inf in foreign
function call (arg 4)

The error does not show up if I stratify the data into
three time slices with varying area connectivity, but
shows up again if I stratify, but leave area
connectivity as 1 for all area combinations in all the
slices. I would be grateful for any suggestions on how
to solve this.

The same script runs with the Psychotria data without
errors, so it seems to be related to my data, but I
can't figure out why it runs when I stratify, but not
when I don't.

I would also appreciate to be added to the BioGeoBEAR
google group.

Thanks,
X

Date: Fri, 14 Feb 2014 22:27:35 -0500
From: Nick Matzke <mat...@nimbios.org>
To: X
CC: mat...@nimbios.org <mat...@nimbios.org>

Hi!

Your best bet is to change the min/max bounds on d/e/j so
they are a little further from 0 or the theoretical max,
usually NaNs occur when the optimx package tries to explore
some value that causes some super-small
calculated probability that (this is my guess) causes a
precision underrun and gets misread as negative...

If that doesn't work you can send me the files and I can try
debugging.

Cheers! Nick

messages.author: 115d05260b0c341a
messages.subject: meaning of "d", "e", "j", "y", "s" and "v"
parts:
On Friday, March 7, 2014 5:20:44 PM UTC-5, emharrower wrote:
This is a question that shows my incompetence in R. How do I query the results to find out what the final values of "y", "s" and "v" were. Do the values of "d", "e", "j", "y", "s" and "v" tell me about the relative importance of each process?

Emma

Howdy!

The values of "d", "e", "j", "y", "s" and "v" are available in the parameters table.  In the input BioGeoBEARS_run_object object (before ML analysis), the parameters table is at:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table

...in the results output object, typically res or resDEC or resDECj depending on where you are in the script, the parameters table is at:

res$outputs@params_table

To access a specific value:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$BioGeoBEARS_model_object@params_table["j","est"]

res$outputs@params_table["j","est"]

...etc.


In the example DEC+J analysis, for example, you can see that the "est" column has changed, but the "init" column has not.


In params_table, the columns mean:

=============
type: is the parameter free or fixed, or controlled by a formula?

init: initial starting value in ML search - specified by defaults or by user

min/max: minimum and maximum values that the ML search is allowed to explore. Sometimes, crashes can be avoided by moving e.g. the min slightly further from 0.

est: the estimated parameter value after ML search.  Before search, this is the same as "init" (unless the user changed it)

note: Comments from me about whether this parameter works, i.e. is fully implemented in the code

desc: Description of the parameter
=============

Column "desc" will tell you basically what "d", "e", "j", "y", "s" and "v" mean.  

"d" and "e" are rates per million years along branches

"j", "y", "s" and "v" are "per-event weights" *per speciation event*.  They are NOT probabilities or rates, and so are not directly comparable to "d" and "e".  To see how probabilities are calculated from the weights, see this Excel spreadsheet:

https://googledrive.com/host/0B6HJElw5txrwZlhjQ0ZUcEdzUG8/ch2_SuppData_01_cladogenesis_parameterizations_v03.xlsx

Yes, the weights thing is slightly weird.  But it's not my fault, it's product of the DEC cladogenesis model of Ree & Smith 2008.  And it's not their fault either, there actually is not an obviously better way to do it, because you have different numbers of different types of cladogenesis events, dependent on the ancestral range size (e.g. you can't have vicariance when the ancestor is range size 1; you can't have jump dispersal when the range size is all areas; etc.).  Several phylogeneticists have independently suggested to me that a simplex formulation would be preferable, but I can't see a way to make this work in practice due to the different-range-sizes-have-different-possible-descendant-event-counts issue.  It would result in a different model than DEC/DEC+J in any case.

Under DEC, y=s=v=1, and j=0.

Under DEC+J, y=s=v=(3-j)/3, and j can range from 0 to 3.

Of course, I wrote all this so that y, s, v, etc. could each be free parameters, producing various new models, but the behavior of these models has not been explored yet.

If one feels like comparing y,s,v,j to d and e, the best way to do it would be to estimate the speciation rate on your phylogeny with e.g. geiger, then calculate the probabilities of all cladogenesis events conditional on each possible ancestor, then multiply each of these probabilities by the speciation rate.  But this would rapidly get too complex to display easily. And you would have to think about base frequencies of states, something currently ignored in these models and probably not solvable except null ranges are excluded, or in a full SSE-type model.

A better method would just be to statistically compare the models where cladogenesis processes are "on" (DEC, DEC+J, etc.) with a model where they are all off (BayArea, or really I should call it BAYAREALIKE, since it's a likelihood representation of BayArea's implied cladogenesis model, not a complete replication of everything BayArea does).  This is done in the example script.  If BayArea comes out as the best model, then the cladogenesis processes were not useful explainers of your geographic range data.


Graphical version of which events each parameter controls:

Update November 12, 2013: BioGeoBEARS in one slide
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears#toc5

Cheers,
Nick
